title: MindCare+: A Digital Phenotyping Framework for Mental Health Monitoring and Support in Indonesia
content: Background: Indonesia has a substantial adolescent mental health burden and a large service gap. The Indonesia-National Adolescent Mental Health Survey estimated that 34.9% of adolescents had a mental health problem and 5.5% met criteria for a mental disorder in the previous 12 months [1,2]. Only 2.6% of adolescents with a mental health problem had accessed support or counselling services [1]. Smartphone and wearable sensing can capture longitudinal behavioral and physiological signals, but current digital phenotyping evidence is heterogeneous and remains constrained by missingness, limited external validation, and uncertain clinical utility [3–7]. Objective: To reformulate the original MindCare+ student innovation concept into an evidence-bounded, human-supervised research architecture for longitudinal mental health risk monitoring and stepped psychological support in Indonesia. Methods: We used an evidence-informed conceptual framework-development approach. The original proposal was decomposed into sensing, interpretation, screening, support, professional integration, governance, and implementation domains. Targeted literature was used to classify proposed functions as near-term capabilities, translational hypotheses, or functions that should not be assumed without prospective validation. No participant-level data were generated and no efficacy analysis was performed. Results: MindCare+ is specified as a consent-based closed loop linking smartphone-derived behavioral features, optional wearable physiology, active validated self-report, data-quality and privacy gating, longitudinal personal baselines, contextual multimodal interpretation, visible uncertainty, stepped support, and human escalation. Passive signals are treated as risk-relevant context rather than psychiatric labels. Active screening is used as an additional assessment layer rather than a diagnosis. A staged validation pathway is proposed from data capture reliability and psychometric localization through prospective clinical comparison, human-factors testing, fairness and privacy evaluation, and controlled implementation. Conclusions: MindCare+ should be evaluated as a research program rather than as an autonomous mental health detector. Its central testable question is whether privacy-preserving longitudinal sensing, combined with active screening and meaningful human oversight, can improve recognition of clinically relevant change and access to appropriate support without producing unacceptable false alerts, surveillance burden, inequity, or harm.
